title: Anti-N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor encephalitis in a patient with a 7-year history of being diagnosed as schizophrenia: complexities in diagnosis and treatment
case_prompt:
A 25-year-old woman with a 7-year history of schizophrenia presented with acute-onset psychotic symptoms. Fifteen days before admission, she developed insomnia, and on the day before admission she felt as if she were traveling through space and time and could not recognize her parents or distinguish colors. She then exhibited intermittent restlessness, excitement, loud yelling with expressions of sadness, suicidal and homicidal ideation, and refusal to sleep or to be hospitalized. On examination, she stood and walked unstably and had palmar sweating; otherwise, her vital signs and neurologic examination were unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies were normal. An electroencephalogram showed mild abnormality, and brain MRI revealed a small ischemic focus in the left frontal lobe; both findings were considered nonspecific. 

A relapse of schizophrenia was first presumed, and ziprasidone (120 mg/day) with irregular haloperidol or olanzapine was administered to control aggression. Two weeks later, modified electroconvulsive therapy (MECT) was given because the psychiatric symptoms had not been relieved. After one MECT session, she developed fluctuating consciousness, fever, sweating, carphology, orofacial dyskinetic movements, bed-wetting, visual hallucinations, amnesia, and intermittent hypermyotonia. Chest and abdominal CT showed left lower-lobe pneumonia. Blood tests revealed a leukocyte count of 19.94 × 10^6/L, creatine kinase of 2223 IU/L, and lactate dehydrogenase of 707 IU/L. Atypical neuroleptic malignant syndrome and an organic brain disorder were considered, and all psychotropic medications and MECT were stopped. 

A lumbar puncture showed pleocytosis (10 × 10^6 white cells/L) with normal biochemistry and negative bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal smears.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Schizophrenia relapse was considered but poor response to standard treatment argued against it — “A relapse of schizophrenia was first considered ... Two weeks later, modified electroconvulsive therapy (MECT) was administered because the psychiatric symptoms had not been relieved.”  
2. Atypical neuroleptic malignant syndrome was considered given autonomic instability, fever, elevated CK, and movement abnormalities — “Based on the clinical features, atypical neuroleptic malignant syndrome and an organic disorder of the brain were considered.”  
3. Viral encephalitis was empirically treated given CSF pleocytosis and clinical features — “Empirical treatment with acyclovir and sodium valproate was administered.”  
4. Anti-NMDAR encephalitis was confirmed by detection of specific IgG NR1 antibodies in CSF — “the tests for autoimmune encephalitis antibodies ... were positive for NMDAR-Ab ... The diagnosis was revised to anti-NMDAR encephalitis.”
